title: THE KING WAS CHOSEN. THE CROWD WAS WAITING. BUT SAUL WAS HIDING IN THE BAGGAGE.
paragraphs: THE KING WAS CHOSEN. THE CROWD WAS WAITING. BUT SAUL WAS HIDING IN THE BAGGAGE.
The disturbing story of Saul’s coronation—and what happens when God’s calling finds a frightened man hiding where nobody thought to look.
Imagine hearing your name called in front of an entire nation.
Not for a punishment.
Not for an accusation.
For a crown.

Thousands of eyes are waiting to see the man who will become Israel’s first human king. The prophet Samuel is there. The tribes have assembled before the LORD. The selection has narrowed from Israel… to Benjamin… from Benjamin to a particular family… and finally to one man.
Saul son of Kish.
The moment has arrived.
The future king should step forward.
Except there is one problem.
Nobody can find him.
The man chosen to stand above the nation is nowhere to be seen.
People begin searching.
Samuel has already privately anointed him. Saul has already received extraordinary confirming signs. The Spirit of God has already come powerfully upon him. Saul has already prophesied.
And now, when the public moment finally comes…
he disappears.
So Israel does something almost unbelievable.
They ask God where their king is.
And God answers.
The ancient Hebrew preserves the scene with almost painful simplicity:
הִנֵּה־הוּא נֶחְבָּא אֶל־הַכֵּלִים
Hinnēh-hū neḥbāʾ el-ha-kēlîm.
“Behold, he is hiding among the baggage.”
—1 Samuel 10:22
There he is.
The king.
In the baggage.
Sit with that image for a moment.
A crown is waiting for him while he is hiding among supplies.
A nation is looking for him while he is trying not to be seen.
His name has been called, but fear—or perhaps overwhelming reluctance—has driven him into hiding.
And maybe that is why this ancient coronation suddenly feels painfully modern.
Because some of us know exactly what it means to hide.
We just have better baggage.
We hide behind work.
Behind humor.
Behind ministry.
Behind “I’m fine.”
Behind achievement.
Behind theological knowledge.
Behind the opinions of other people.
Behind old wounds.
Behind the memory of what we did.
Behind what somebody did to us.
Behind the fear that if people really knew us, they would walk away.
Some people even hide behind religion.
We can sing while hiding.
Serve while hiding.
Preach while hiding.
Post Bible verses while hiding.
Tell everyone else that God is faithful while privately wondering whether He could possibly still want anything to do with us.
The baggage has changed.
The hiding has not.
But to understand Saul’s moment correctly, we have to resist turning this passage into a shallow motivational slogan.
This is not merely, “Stop hiding because you are destined for greatness.”
The Bible is telling a far more sobering story.
Israel’s request for a king was itself spiritually complicated.
Before Saul was publicly selected, Samuel reminded Israel that God had delivered them from Egypt and rescued them from their oppressors, yet they had demanded, “Set a king over us.”
Israel already had a King.
The LORD.
And yet they wanted a king they could see.
A king like the nations around them.
Then comes Saul.
And from the human perspective, he looks spectacular.
When they finally drag him out from among the baggage and place him before the people, Scripture says he stands taller than everyone else.
Samuel announces:
“Do you see the one whom the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.”
And the crowd erupts:
יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ
Yeḥi ha-melekh.
“Long live the king!”
What a scene.
The hidden man is suddenly standing above everybody.
The frightened man is surrounded by cheers.
The man behind the baggage is now at the center of the nation.
But if you know Saul’s story, those cheers hurt.
Because you know what comes later.
You know that Saul’s beginning will not guarantee his ending.
You know the man hiding from the crown will eventually become a man desperately clinging to the throne.
That is one of the tragedies of Saul.
At the beginning, he seems small in his own eyes.
Later, when obedience becomes costly, his relationship with power becomes something very different.
The man who once had to be pulled out of hiding will eventually fear losing what he once seemed afraid to possess.
And somewhere inside that transformation is a warning for every Christian.
Humility is not merely thinking little of yourself.
And insecurity is not automatically holiness.
Sometimes what looks like humility can coexist with a heart still governed by the opinions of people.
Saul’s later story exposes this painfully.
After his disobedience concerning Amalek, Saul eventually admits to Samuel:
“I have sinned. I violated the LORD’s command and your instructions. I was afraid of the people and obeyed their voice.”
—1 Samuel 15:24
There it is.
The crowd.
The same human eyes that once watched his coronation would become voices he feared disappointing.
And suddenly the baggage scene becomes even more haunting.
Because sometimes we come out of physical hiding without ever coming out of heart-level hiding.
You can stand in front of everyone and still be imprisoned by what everyone thinks.
You can wear the crown and still be afraid.
You can have the title and still need approval.
You can become successful and still be controlled by the terrified person you were before anybody knew your name.
Maybe that is where this story finds you.
Not behind literal baggage.
Behind emotional baggage.
The childhood that still whispers that you are not enough.
The father whose approval you never received.
The relationship that taught you not to trust.
The church wound you never processed.
The secret sin nobody knows about.
The addiction you keep promising will be the last time.
The prayer life that quietly disappeared.
The version of yourself you present publicly versus the person who lies awake at two in the morning.
You learned how to function.
But functioning and freedom are not the same thing.
And here is where we must be careful.
Saul’s story does not teach that every dream in your heart is a divine calling.
It does not promise everybody a throne.
It does not say that believing in yourself will produce your destiny.
Scripture gives us something infinitely better than self-esteem.
It gives us Christ.
Because Saul cannot carry the weight of Israel’s deepest hope.
Neither can David.
Neither can any human ruler.
The Bible keeps moving.
Through failed kings.
Broken kingdoms.
Exile.
Longing.
Prophecy.
Silence.
Until another King arrives.
Jesus Christ.
And the contrast is breathtaking.
Saul was physically impressive.
Jesus was not presented to Israel as the political spectacle many expected.
Saul would eventually disobey God to preserve what mattered to him.
Jesus says of His Father:
“Not my will, but yours, be done.”
Saul feared people.
Jesus walked toward the cross while crowds mocked Him.
Saul desperately tried to preserve his throne.
Jesus willingly surrendered Himself to death.
Saul’s kingship deteriorated beneath disobedience.
Jesus was “obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
And Saul was publicly acclaimed with:
“Long live the king!”
Jesus would eventually stand before another crowd.
Only this crowd would scream something far darker.
“Crucify him!”
Think about the scandal of that.
The true King came.
And humanity crowned Him with thorns.
The hands that formed humanity were pierced by human nails.
The One without sin was condemned among sinners.
The innocent Son of God carried a cross through streets filled with people He came to save.
And at Calvary, something happened infinitely greater than Saul emerging from the baggage.
Jesus carried ours.
Not suitcases.
Sin.
Guilt.
Condemnation.
Shame.
Our rebellion against God.
Our secret darkness.
Our religious hypocrisy.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our pride.
Our lies.
Our self-righteousness.
Our attempts to become our own kings.
He carried what we could never remove from ourselves.
“For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”
—1 Peter 3:18
That is the Gospel.
Not God discovering that you were secretly wonderful all along.
God loving sinners at unimaginable cost.
Not Jesus helping good people become slightly better.
Jesus dying for the guilty and rising victorious so sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
Grace does not pretend the baggage is empty.
Grace opens it.
Grace exposes what sin has done.
Grace calls sin what God calls it.
Then grace points trembling sinners toward a blood-stained cross and an empty tomb and says:
There is mercy here.
Maybe you have spent years hiding something.
You know exactly what it is.
Nobody reading this needs to know.
But God already does.
That sentence may terrify you.
It should also give you hope.
Because the God who knows where Saul is hiding knows where you are hiding too.
When Israel could not find Saul, God could.
“Behold, he is hiding among the baggage.”
There was no corner obscure enough to escape His sight.
And neither is yours.
Psalm 139 asks:
“Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?”
The answer is nowhere.
But for the person who comes to Christ, that is not merely terrifying news.
It is beautiful news.
Because the One from whom you cannot hide is the very One who invites sinners to come into the light.
You do not need to clean every piece of baggage before approaching Jesus.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
You repent.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
You stop negotiating.
You stop pretending.
You bring the truth into His light.
And you trust the crucified and risen Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be true.
“Jesus, I’m tired of hiding.”
There are people reading this who have been carrying something so long that it has started feeling like part of their identity.
It is not.
Your sin is serious.
Your wounds are real.
Your failures have consequences.
But none of them gets to be your Savior.
Jesus does.
And if you belong to Him, your worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence.
That belongs to Christ.
This is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the mercy of God calling you away from destruction.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
Saul’s life warns us that a powerful beginning does not make obedience optional.
Anointing is not permission for rebellion.
Spiritual experiences are not substitutes for faithfulness.
Public applause is not evidence that everything is healthy inside.
And yesterday’s encounter with God cannot become an excuse for today’s disobedience.
The question is not merely whether God has used you.
The question is whether your heart belongs to Him.
Because there is something more frightening than being found hiding among baggage.
It is eventually standing before everyone while your heart remains hidden from surrender.
So be honest.
What are you hiding behind?
What are you protecting that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
What opinion matters so much that you have started compromising obedience?
What secret would collapse the image you have spent years constructing?
What baggage has become comfortable enough that you almost forgot it was hiding you?
You might forget this article.
Do not forget that question.
And if the Holy Spirit is exposing something in you through Scripture, do not bury it beneath another distraction.
Bring it to Christ.
Today.
Not after you become worthy.
You cannot make yourself worthy.
Come because Jesus is worthy.
Come because His blood is sufficient.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because grace is still grace.
Come because the King you actually need is not Saul.
His name is Jesus.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by financial support, social-media engagement, or religious works.

But if this ministry is faithfully helping people encounter Scripture and hear the Gospel, supporting and sharing that work can be one practical way to participate in putting biblical truth in front of people who may never walk into a church.
It does not buy His favor.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be a voluntary act of generosity that helps more Scripture-centered content and discipleship resources reach people who desperately need them.
But whether you ever give a cent or not, hear this clearly:
Do not hide from Jesus.
The baggage cannot forgive you.
The applause cannot heal you.
The title cannot save you.
The image cannot cleanse you.
The crowd cannot tell you who you ultimately are.
Run to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Walk in the light.
And when grace pulls you out of hiding, do not crawl back into the baggage Jesus died to free you from.
Because sometimes the most dangerous hiding place is not where nobody can see you—it is where everybody can see you, but nobody knows you are still hiding.
